lessons.title: What is a share?
lessons.summary: Understand what you own when you buy part of a business.
outcomes: Explain ownership in plain language
Separate a business from its share price
Recognise that a return is not guaranteed

sections.heading: A small slice of a business
sections.text: A share is an ownership interest in a company. Owning a share is different from lending the company money: shareholders participate in the business’s fortunes and bear the risk of loss.

sections.heading: Price and business are related, but different
sections.text: A company may make useful products while its shares still offer poor value at a particular price. Buying because you recognise a name does not tell you how much the business is worth.

sections.heading: Where a return may come from
sections.text: An investor may receive dividends or sell at a different price. Neither outcome is certain. A rising price is an unrealised gain until you sell; a falling price can become a permanent loss.

sections.heading: A business needs money; an investor needs an explanation
sections.text:
Imagine a small milling company that wants to buy a second machine. It could retain profits, borrow, or raise money from owners. These choices create different claims on the business. A lender expects payments under a contract. An ordinary shareholder owns a residual interest: what remains for owners after the business meets its obligations. That distinction helps explain why a successful business may reward shareholders, while a struggling one may pay them nothing. Ownership is a claim with uncertainty, rather than a promise that a particular amount will arrive on a particular date.

Also distinguish a new share issue from a trade between investors. When a company issues new shares for cash, the company receives that money. When one investor sells existing shares to another, the seller normally receives the sale proceeds. The listed company does not receive fresh money every time its shares change hands. Before researching a company, practise explaining where the money in a proposed transaction goes, what the buyer receives, and which rights or obligations come with that instrument. A familiar company name alone cannot answer those questions.

sections.heading: Count ownership in proportions, not just share certificates
sections.text:
Suppose an imaginary company has 10,000 ordinary shares outstanding and you own 100. Your proportion is 100 divided by 10,000, or 1%. If the company later issues another 10,000 shares and you do not acquire any, your 100 shares represent 0.5% of the enlarged total. This is dilution of your percentage ownership. It does not by itself tell you whether the new financing is good or bad: the company may receive valuable resources that help the business, or it may use the money poorly. Both the denominator and the business consequences matter.

A share split illustrates a different change. In a two-for-one split, your 100 shares become 200 while the total number of shares also doubles. Your percentage ownership remains the same. Doubling the number of units in your account does not automatically double your wealth. These examples show why the number of shares, their quoted price and the proportion of the company are separate quantities. Whenever someone says a share is cheap because its unit price is small, ask how many shares exist and what the whole business is being valued at.

sections.heading: Rights do not mean day-to-day control
sections.text:
Ordinary shares can carry voting rights and a right to participate in distributions, but the exact rights depend on the share class and company documents. An individual shareholder usually does not decide the daily price of a product, employ staff or withdraw cash from the company's bank account. Management runs the operation under its governance structure. Shareholders use the rights available to them through the proper channels, such as receiving information and voting on relevant matters. Read the instrument's terms rather than assuming that every security labelled a share has identical rights.

Think carefully about what limited liability does and does not mean. In the usual case of fully paid ordinary shares bought without borrowing, the shareholder can lose the amount invested without being personally responsible for all the company's debts merely because they own shares. That does not protect the market value of the investment. It also does not cancel obligations under a separate loan, guarantee or leveraged arrangement the investor has entered. Our classroom buys ordinary practice shares with virtual cash. It does not model borrowing, personal guarantees, derivatives or every possible security structure.

sections.heading: Follow the money when measuring a return
sections.text:
Use a complete small example. A learner imagines buying 100 shares at KES 20, spending KES 2,000 before costs. The company later pays an assumed KES 1 dividend per share, producing KES 100 of gross income. If the shares could then be sold at KES 18, the sale value would be KES 1,800. Income of KES 100 does not erase the KES 200 price loss: the combined result is a KES 100 loss before costs and tax. Receiving a payment and making an overall profit are different observations.

If the sale price were KES 23 instead, the same simplified calculation would give KES 300 of price gain plus KES 100 of dividends. That is KES 400 on a KES 2,000 purchase, or 20%, before costs and tax. These are invented outcomes for arithmetic, not expected returns. While the shares remain unsold, a quoted value is an estimate of current market value, not cash already received. A real sale may occur at a different price. Keep ownership, cash received, current value and a realised sale result separate in your notes.

sections.heading: Turn recognition into a research question
sections.text:
A business you use every day can be a useful starting point because you understand part of its product. It is still only a starting point. Ask who pays the business, what costs it must cover, whether it owes money, and what could make customers leave. A popular product can coexist with weak finances or an expensive share price. Conversely, an unfamiliar name might operate a sound business that still requires investigation. Research replaces recognition with evidence; it does not require inventing certainty where information is missing.

Create a first research note with five sentences: what the business sells, who its customers are, one piece of evidence you have checked, one risk you cannot yet assess, and one question for further reading. Keep facts separate from guesses. For example, “the annual report shows revenue for the year ended June” is different from “I think demand will rise next year.” Record the date and source of the fact. At this stage, a useful learning outcome is a clearer question, not a decision to buy. The later classes add accounts, costs, valuation and execution to this foundation.

example.title: An imaginary bakery
example.text:
Suppose a bakery has 1,000 equal shares and you own 10. You own 1% of its shares. If it declares a KES 2 dividend per share, your gross dividend would be KES 20. It may also declare no dividend.

Take the bakery example further. Imagine that you buy the ten shares for KES 100 each, spending KES 1,000 before costs. A KES 20 gross dividend arrives, but the best hypothetical sale price later is KES 90 per share. Sale value is KES 900; adding the dividend produces KES 920. Compared with the purchase, that is a KES 80 loss before omitted costs and tax. The bakery might still be operating and selling bread. Your investment outcome depends on the price paid, subsequent value and distributions, not simply on whether the product remains useful. Now imagine that the company raises new capital. Ask how many new shares are issued, what resources the business receives and how your ownership fraction changes. These are separate questions. Write the calculation and the missing information together so a familiar business story does not hide the actual arithmetic.

lessons.summary: Learn the roles of the exchange, regulator, broker and depository.
outcomes: Identify four market participants

sections.heading: Who does what?
sections.text: The Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE) provides a marketplace. A licensed intermediary handles client orders. CDSC maintains electronic securities records through its systems and agents. The Capital Markets Authority (CMA) regulates Kenya’s capital markets.

sections.heading: Verify before you trust
sections.text: Check an intermediary’s exact legal name on the CMA register. A logo in an advert, a popular app or a social-media following is not independent evidence of authorisation.

sections.heading: Read the whole market picture
sections.text: A market index summarises a selected basket of shares. Its movement does not mean every company has risen or fallen by the same amount. Learn which companies and weighting method an index uses.

sections.heading: Separate the institutions before following a headline
sections.text:
Several institutions can appear in a single investing journey, so give each a clear role in your notebook. The exchange provides a marketplace and publishes market or issuer information. An intermediary handles the services it is authorised to offer to customers. The depository and its agents provide the relevant securities-record infrastructure and account services. The regulator supervises activities within its remit and provides official information on licensing and investor protection. None of these roles should be assumed to guarantee that a share will rise or that a particular decision suits your finances.

Test your understanding with a fictional problem. Your account shows an unexpected transaction, and a social-media post says that “the NSE app” will fix it if you send a password. Pause. Identify the actual provider that holds your account relationship and use verified contact details. An institution's name in a message is not proof that the message came from it. Clear role labels make it easier to ask the right organisation the right question and to spot requests that do not fit the relationship you actually have.

sections.heading: A trade is a process, not one screen tap
sections.text:
The visible order button is only one part of a transaction. A customer gives an instruction, the provider checks the instruction and available resources, and an order may then interact with the market. Execution means a trade has been matched under the relevant arrangements. Settlement completes the agreed delivery of securities and money. Recording and reconciling the resulting holdings is another part of the process. The precise timing, supported order types and customer procedures must come from the current intermediary and official market guidance.

Our practice screen compresses this process into an immediate change in cash and shares. That simplification is useful for learning quantities, but it can hide delays and failures that matter in real life. An order might be rejected, wait, fill partly, or not fill. A balance or screen message can refer to available funds, unsettled activity or an account record rather than the same thing in every system. When you see a new label, write down what it means before treating it as money ready to withdraw or shares ready to sell.

sections.heading: An index describes a basket, not your own result
sections.text:
A market index combines selected securities according to a published method. To interpret it, ask which securities are included, how they are weighted and whether the quoted series includes distributions. If a large constituent moves strongly, an index can rise even while several smaller companies fall. A headline about an index is therefore not a statement about every listed business. It also is not the return earned by a learner who holds a different combination of shares or who bought and sold on different dates.

Consider a fictional basket with 80% in Company A and 20% in Company B. If A rises 5% and B falls 5%, the weighted movement is 4% minus 1%, or 3%, ignoring other features. Simply averaging the two percentage moves would produce 0% and miss the weights. This example is not the methodology of a particular Kenyan index. It is a way to see why an index name, weighting method, date range and calculation basis all belong beside the number. Ask those questions before using an index to compare an investment outcome.

sections.heading: Verify a service rather than trusting its presentation
sections.text:
Begin a provider check with the exact legal name and the service being offered. A brand, an app name and a regulated legal entity may not be the same wording. Look up the entity in the official register and consider whether the listed category matches the proposed activity. Then compare independently published contact details with those used in the approach you received. Do not send passwords, one-time codes or payment merely because a website uses an official logo or repeats a registration number.

Keep a dated record of what you checked and what remains unclear. Registration is one question; the actual account terms, ownership structure, costs, funding methods, order service and complaint route are additional questions. A licence check does not replace reading those terms, and a useful interface does not replace a licence check. If a claimed affiliation or account structure cannot be explained clearly, stop the process and ask through a verified channel. “I have not established this yet” is a responsible note, not a failure to keep up with other investors.

sections.heading: Build a small evidence trail for every market claim
sections.text:
When a claim appears in a video, group chat or headline, trace it to a document when possible. For a company result, look for the issuer's report or announcement and identify the period covered. For a procedure, look for the relevant institution's current guidance. For a provider's charge, obtain the provider's own tariff and terms. These sources answer different questions. A company report cannot establish a broker's commission, and a general overseas explainer cannot establish the current account procedure in Kenya.

A useful record has the claim, the source title, the publication or reporting date, the date you checked it, and your interpretation. Preserve units: KES, thousands of KES, millions of KES and percentages are not interchangeable. Also preserve uncertainty. A management forecast should not be rewritten as a result that has already happened. In this classroom, original explanations and invented examples sit beside credited references. Follow that same habit in your own research so that another learner can see what you observed, how you interpreted it and what you still need to verify.

example.title: One market, different outcomes
example.text:
In a two-company illustration, one share rises 5% while another falls 5%. An index could still move up if the first company carries more weight. A headline about “the market” is not a result for every investor.

Add a source check to the two-company example. Suppose one headline reports a three-percent index rise while a learner's only share falls five percent. There is no necessary contradiction: the learner's holding and the index basket are different. Ask for the index's constituents, weights and dates before trying to reconcile them. Then imagine a message offering to open an account through “an exchange partner.” List the exact legal entity, claimed service, official register entry and independently verified contact route you would need. A market headline cannot verify that provider. Finally, choose an issuer announcement and record its title, reporting period and units. Explain which organisation produced each piece of evidence and which question it answers. This exercise connects institutional roles with practical research, without asking you to select a provider, predict a price or treat the index movement as a personal return.

lessons.title: How buying & selling works
lessons.summary: Follow an order from your instruction to a completed transaction.
outcomes: Explain market and limit orders
Distinguish execution from settlement
Use the practice order screen

sections.heading: Give a clear instruction
sections.text: A buy or sell instruction includes the security, quantity and order conditions. A market order seeks execution at available prices; a limit order places a price boundary. Ask your intermediary which order types are supported.

sections.heading: An order is not a completed trade
sections.text: A limit order may not fill. An order can also fill in parts. Liquidity and price changes affect what is available. A displayed quote does not promise that every share you request can trade at that price.

sections.heading: What happens afterwards
sections.text: Execution is when a trade is matched; settlement completes the exchange of cash and securities. Keep contract notes and check statements. Confirm current settlement arrangements with the intermediary rather than assuming the simulator’s instant fill applies.

sections.heading: Specify the instruction before discussing the price
sections.text:
A complete order description needs more than “buy that company.” Identify the security, direction, quantity, order type and any relevant price boundary or duration. Check the provider's terminology because similar labels can have different conditions. For a buy, consider whether sufficient funds are available for both the purchase and charges. For a sale, establish that the shares are held and available under the account's rules. Do not assume a display of total portfolio value means the same amount can fund a new order immediately.

Practise speaking an instruction back in plain language. “Buy 20 shares, subject to a maximum price of KES 50 per share, using the supported limit-order service” communicates a different intention from seeking immediate execution at the available market price. This is a hypothetical description, not a statement that every provider supports that exact service. Before placing an actual order, resolve any disagreement between your intention, the platform's preview and the provider's explanation. An unclear instruction should be corrected before it becomes an executed transaction.

sections.heading: A quote is information; an execution is an outcome
sections.text:
The last traded price tells you about a completed trade at a particular time. It is not a promise that another buyer or seller will be available at that price when your order arrives. The bid represents a quoted buying interest and the offer or ask a selling interest, subject to the information service and market conditions. The difference between them is the spread. The quantity available at a price matters as well: a large order can consume several levels of available liquidity.

Imagine an order for 100 shares when only 40 are offered at KES 50 and another 60 at KES 51. If those offers are available when an eligible market order executes, the gross cost would be 40 times 50 plus 60 times 51, or KES 5,060. The average execution price is KES 50.60. A screen showing KES 50 did not guarantee a KES 5,000 purchase. This simplified order-book example omits timing, other instructions and costs, but it explains why price, quantity and execution conditions need to be considered together.

sections.heading: Price control and execution certainty are different aims
sections.text:
A market order seeks execution at available prices; the eventual price can differ from what was on screen. A limit order sets a boundary, but it can wait or remain unfilled. Neither label removes every risk. The appropriate instruction depends on the supported service, the security and the investor's actual objective. Do not select an order type only because its name sounds safer. Ask what can happen if the market moves, there is little liquidity or the order reaches the system later than expected.

For an invented buy limit of KES 50, offers above KES 50 are outside the boundary. If no qualifying shares are available, the correct result may be no purchase at all. A learner who then increases the limit repeatedly is changing the decision and should record why. The order's duration also matters: a waiting instruction may remain active under its terms after the original reason has changed. Check the provider's rules for expiry, amendments and cancellation, and distinguish a cancellation request from confirmation that the instruction has actually been cancelled.

sections.heading: Reconcile the record instead of repeating an uncertain order
sections.text:
An interrupted connection or delayed screen message creates uncertainty about status, not proof that nothing happened. Repeating an instruction without checking can produce an unintended second order. Use the provider's status information, transaction records and verified support route to establish what was received and executed. Keep the time, security, quantity and reference details needed for a factual query. Do not share passwords or authentication codes with someone who offers to investigate through an unsolicited message.

After a real transaction, compare the relevant confirmation or contract note with your instruction, account activity and eventual holdings record. Examine quantities, prices, charges and dates rather than checking only whether the total looks familiar. Execution and settlement need not be the same event. If there is a discrepancy, document it and use the appropriate provider and official complaint process. Our simulator has no connection failure or settlement delay model. Its instant success message teaches arithmetic, but it must not become an expectation that every real-world instruction follows the same path.

sections.heading: Use the simulator as a controlled experiment
sections.text:
Begin with a small virtual order so that you can explain each change. Buying ten illustrative shares at KES 25 uses KES 250 and adds ten shares to holdings. Selling four at the same fixed practice price returns KES 100 and leaves six shares. Because the simulator keeps its example price fixed and uses zero practice fees, those actions do not demonstrate a profitable trading strategy. They demonstrate the connection between quantity, price, cash and holdings under deliberately simplified assumptions.

Write down what is missing from the experiment: a moving market, a spread, actual commissions, taxes, partial fills, settlement and possible order-service restrictions. Then use the fee calculator to investigate one omitted cost separately. Changing one assumption at a time makes it easier to understand the result. If the practice screen rejects a sale larger than your holdings, explain that boundary rather than trying random quantities until an order passes. A useful practice trade ends with an account you can reconcile and a short note about what the exercise did and did not test.

example.title: A price boundary
example.text:
Imagine you want 20 shares and set a buy limit of KES 30. Your price ceiling is KES 30, excluding costs. If the lowest available seller wants KES 31, the order may remain unfilled.

Extend the order exercise with a ledger. Start with KES 1,000 of imaginary cash, buy ten shares at KES 25 and then sell four at the same fixed price. The purchase uses KES 250, leaving KES 750 and ten shares. The sale returns KES 100, leaving KES 850 and six shares. At the unchanged example price, the remaining shares are worth KES 150, so cash plus shares still totals KES 1,000 before omitted costs. This is reconciliation, not a trading profit. Next assume a connection fails after a real instruction is sent. You cannot tell from the missing screen message alone whether the order was received or executed. Describe the status checks and records you would obtain before repeating it. Keep that uncertainty separate from the simple cash arithmetic; an accurate multiplication does not establish the state of a real order.

lessons.summary: Build habits for uncertainty before thinking about profits.

sections.heading: Start with the money’s purpose
sections.text: Money for an expense due soon has a different job from money intended for a distant goal. Consider what happens if the value falls just before you need to withdraw it.

sections.heading: Risk is more than a price chart
sections.text: A business can lose customers, take on too much debt or face disruption. Investors also face market-wide events and difficulty selling. Being comfortable with uncertainty does not make a loss affordable.

sections.heading: Use a process you can repeat
sections.text: Set a review routine, record your reasons, and avoid decisions made only because prices moved today. Diversification can reduce exposure to one business but cannot remove every risk or guarantee a profit.

sections.heading: Begin with consequences, not with a target return
sections.text:
Risk becomes more concrete when you describe the consequence of being wrong. Money needed soon for an essential bill serves a different purpose from money that could remain invested for a long period. A temporary price fall can still create a permanent problem if it forces a sale at an unsuitable time. Before discussing a desired return, describe the goal, the date when the money may be needed, and what would happen if the investment were worth less at that point.

Separate willingness from capacity. A person may feel comfortable with uncertainty but be unable to absorb a loss because the money funds important obligations. Another person may have financial capacity but dislike large price movements. Neither issue is solved by copying someone else's allocation or by choosing a fashionable share. This classroom cannot assess your personal circumstances. It can help you ask better questions about timing, access to cash and loss consequences, and recognise when those questions require more information or individual professional guidance.

sections.heading: Identify several risks rather than one price forecast
sections.text:
Business risk concerns the operation itself: demand, costs, competition, management decisions and financing can all affect results. Market prices can also move because investors change their expectations or the price they are willing to pay. Liquidity risk concerns the ability to trade an amount when needed without an unacceptable price effect. Concentration connects several outcomes to the same source of exposure. There can also be provider, operational and fraud concerns that cannot be evaluated by looking only at a company's chart.

Choose an imaginary retailer and write one possible problem in each category. A supplier interruption affects the business. A thin market can complicate a sale even if the retailer's shops are operating normally. An account-access problem creates a different obstacle again. These examples do not predict that any event will occur. They train you to consider more than one way a plan can fail. When reviewing a decision, ask which risk you actually investigated and which you merely assumed away because the recent price had looked reassuring.

sections.heading: Concentration can be hidden behind several names
sections.text:
Owning several securities does not automatically create diverse economic exposure. Two businesses may depend on the same customer group, commodity, interest-rate environment or geographical market. A fund may already hold a share you also own directly. Count the underlying exposures as well as the number of account lines. Diversification can reduce dependence on a particular outcome, but it cannot promise that every holding will rise or that a broad market decline will leave the portfolio unaffected.

Use a fictional portfolio of KES 10,000 with KES 8,000 in one company and KES 2,000 elsewhere. A 25% decline in the larger holding reduces its value by KES 2,000. If the other part is unchanged, the portfolio loses 20%. The company's percentage move and the portfolio's percentage move differ because the position has a weight. This is a useful calculation for understanding exposure. It is not a recommended allocation or a prediction of future price changes. Repeat the arithmetic with different weights and explain the trade-off without calling any arrangement risk-free.

sections.heading: Recovering a loss is not the mirror image of taking it
sections.text:
Start with an invented KES 10,000 investment. A 20% loss leaves KES 8,000. Recovering the missing KES 2,000 now requires a 25% gain on KES 8,000, rather than a 20% gain. The changing base creates this asymmetry. A 50% loss requires a 100% gain to return to the starting amount. These calculations do not say what will happen next; they show why avoiding careless exposure is not the same task as chasing a large percentage return after a loss.

This also explains why averaging percentage returns can mislead. A 20% gain followed by a 20% loss turns KES 10,000 into KES 9,600 before costs, even though the simple average of the two percentages is zero. Apply each period's change to the amount actually present in that period. When someone presents an average return, ask how it was calculated, whether money moved in or out, and whether costs were included. A striking number without a calculation basis is an invitation to investigate, not a reliable result.

sections.heading: Build habits that make decisions reviewable
sections.text:
A repeatable routine can include checking a source, recording an assumption, comparing costs and deciding when the evidence is insufficient. The routine does not guarantee a good outcome. It gives you a way to distinguish an informed decision from an impulsive one and to learn from both winning and losing outcomes. Waiting is a legitimate result of the routine when important information is missing. It should not be treated as failure merely because another person says they acted quickly.

Try a short pause before a practice order. Write what would make the idea wrong, what loss would mean for the stated goal, and which fact would change your view. After the exercise, return to those statements without rewriting them to fit the result. Watch for social pressure, fear of missing out and a desire to recover a loss immediately. Those feelings can be recorded honestly, but they should not substitute for evidence. The journal later in this course helps you keep the original decision and the later review visible at the same time.

example.title: A concentration check
example.text:
If KES 8,000 of a KES 10,000 portfolio sits in one business, 80% depends on that company. A 25% fall in that holding alone would reduce the full portfolio by KES 2,000, assuming the rest does not move.

Expand the concentration example into a review question. After the larger holding loses KES 2,000, the whole KES 10,000 portfolio is worth KES 8,000 if everything else is unchanged. Returning to KES 10,000 requires a KES 2,000 gain, which is 25% of the remaining KES 8,000. A desire to recover quickly does not supply evidence that such a gain will occur. Write one business risk, one liquidity concern and one consequence of needing the money during the decline. Then ask what information would have been useful before the position was created. A useful answer can identify an exposure that was poorly understood even if you cannot specify exactly how the next market period will behave.

sections.heading: Know the ownership arrangement
sections.text: A CDS account is an electronic securities record. For an individual CDS account, a Central Depository Agent helps with opening and maintenance. If a platform offers another holding structure, ask who is registered as holder and how your entitlement is documented.

sections.heading: Compare the service, not just the app
sections.text: Ask about charges, minimum funding, supported orders, funding and withdrawal steps, statements and support. Request current written terms. Document requirements can differ by provider and by whether you are an individual, company or non-resident.

sections.heading: Keep control of access
sections.text: Use the provider’s verified contact details. Protect passwords and one-time codes. Obtain statements and reconcile holdings against your own records. This classroom account is for learning and is not a CDS or brokerage account.

sections.heading: A classroom login is not a securities account
sections.text:
The account on this website stores lessons, virtual cash and learning notes. It does not create a CDS account, record real securities or authorise real orders. A real-world account relationship involves the relevant provider, required identity checks, documentation and the applicable account structure. Keep these purposes separate even when two products both use an email address and a password. Completing our sign-up process says nothing about your eligibility for a different financial service.

Before opening a real account, ask who the contracting provider is, what service it is authorised to provide and how holdings are recorded. Obtain an explanation you can understand rather than accepting a phrase such as “everything is digital” as a complete answer. Digital access is a method of using a service; it does not establish the legal ownership or custody arrangement by itself. Consult the current CDSC guidance and the intermediary's own documents for the specific arrangement. Do not assume that a classroom example describes every available account model.

sections.heading: Compare the whole service, not only the headline commission
sections.text:
Create a comparison sheet with the same questions for each provider. Include the exact legal name, licence category, account structure, available securities, supported order services, funding and withdrawal arrangements, statements, charges and complaint route. Ask where current tariffs and account terms can be obtained. A low advertised commission can coexist with other charges or limitations that matter to how you intend to use the account. A feature that is valuable to one person may be irrelevant to another.

Use neutral questions rather than a ranking based on social-media popularity. For example: “What record will show my holdings?”, “How can I verify an executed order?”, “What happens if I cannot access the app?” and “Where is a complete schedule of charges?” Record the answer, the document supporting it and the date checked. If a question remains unanswered, leave it marked as unresolved. This classroom does not nominate a best broker. Its purpose is to help you make a comparison that can be examined and updated as services or terms change.

sections.heading: Protect identity and access without outsourcing judgement
sections.text:
Account opening can require personal documents through the provider's authorised process. Before submitting them, establish that you are using the genuine institution and the correct channel. Do not follow a message's embedded link simply because it resembles a familiar name. Compare the domain and contact details with independent official information. Requests to send a password or one-time authentication code to an individual should be treated differently from entering a code into the genuine service you intended to use.

After an account is opened, use the security options the provider supports and keep recovery details current through its proper process. Avoid saving authentication secrets in a learning journal or sharing a screen that exposes them. A fraudster may imitate support staff or claim that an urgent payment is required to release funds. Pause and verify independently. Strong account access habits reduce some operational risks, but they do not determine whether an investment is fairly priced or suitable. Security, provider authorisation and investment judgement are related tasks with different evidence.

sections.heading: Reconcile holdings and cash using the right records
sections.text:
A broker's app, a transaction confirmation and a holdings statement may display different aspects of activity. Learn what each record covers and when it updates. Compare security identifiers, quantities, prices, charges and relevant dates. Do not assume that a screenshot of a portfolio total proves how every security is recorded. Ask the provider and the depository's current guidance how you should obtain and interpret the records relevant to your account structure.

For a fictional purchase of 30 shares followed by a sale of 10, begin by expecting 20 shares, then reconcile the actual records rather than treating that mental arithmetic as sufficient proof. Check for other activity, pending transactions or relevant adjustments if the records disagree. Preserve copies and reference numbers needed to raise a factual query. Use verified support channels and the applicable complaint procedure. The classroom journal is useful for recording reasoning, but it is not a substitute for an official transaction confirmation or securities-account statement.

sections.heading: Plan the less convenient situations before they occur
sections.text:
A service can be easy to use on a good day yet difficult to understand when circumstances change. Ask about updating details, replacing access credentials, obtaining historical records, transferring holdings or closing an account under the provider's current rules. Consider what information a trusted person would need to locate the provider if you were unable to manage the relationship yourself. Do not place passwords or sensitive identity documents in a shared informal notebook to solve that problem.

Write a simple account-information sheet with the institution's verified contact route, the types of records you keep, and the location of the official terms. Keep sensitive documents separately and appropriately protected. If a concern arises, record the sequence of events and the response received. Follow the relevant institution's published process rather than assuming a social-media complaint reaches the appropriate team. Knowing how records, support and escalation work is part of understanding an account. It deserves attention before the first trade, not only after something has gone wrong.

example.title: Two different account types
example.text:
Your Hisa Classroom login stores completed lessons and virtual shares. It cannot hold real securities, accept deposits or prove ownership of NSE shares. A real provider’s account has a different purpose.

Use a fictional account comparison instead of choosing a real provider. Provider A displays a low headline commission but has not supplied a complete tariff or explained the holdings statement. Provider B supplies more documentation but you still need to verify the legal entity and service category. Neither description is enough to declare a winner. Prepare identical questions for both, list the evidence still required and mark unresolved answers honestly. Then reconcile an imagined record: thirty shares bought, ten sold and no other activity would leave twenty shares, subject to checking the actual statements and transaction records. A different displayed balance calls for investigation, not an automatic accusation or a repeated order. Explain which document would help establish each fact. This creates a practical account-opening checklist while keeping provider verification, investment judgement and record reconciliation as distinct tasks.

lessons.title: Fees & the true cost of a trade
lessons.summary: Work out the cost of buying and later selling.
outcomes: Calculate purchase and sale costs
Understand why frequent trading can be expensive
Separate a price gain from a net gain

sections.heading: Look at both sides
sections.text: A purchase may cost more than quantity multiplied by price. A sale may return less than its headline value. Obtain the intermediary’s current schedule and check commission, levies, minimum charges and any applicable tax.

sections.heading: Use amounts, not just percentages
sections.text: A small percentage can be significant on frequent trades. Minimum charges can matter on smaller orders. Compare the total cash leaving and entering the account, using a written breakdown.

sections.heading: Know the simulator’s limits
sections.text: Our practice orders charge zero fees to make the mechanics easy to learn. The fee explorer below is a separate teaching tool. Its percentages are inputs you choose, not a quoted Kenyan tariff.

sections.heading: Separate the trade amount from the cash actually spent
sections.text:
Quantity times price gives the gross value of a transaction. It does not necessarily give the complete cash outlay or net sale proceeds. A provider may apply percentage charges, fixed charges, minimum amounts or other items under its tariff. Tax treatment and any other applicable costs require current information for the actual situation. Do not treat a simplified example or an old online post as a current Kenyan schedule of charges.

For an invented purchase of 100 shares at KES 20, the gross value is KES 2,000. If a teaching example adds a 2% purchase charge and no other items, the charge is KES 40 and cash outlay is KES 2,040. The 2% is an assumption chosen for arithmetic, not a quoted market rate. Write that assumption beside the result. When moving from an example to a real tariff, check exactly which base each charge uses and whether the tariff has conditions that the classroom calculation has deliberately left out.

sections.heading: Work through both sides before calling a trade profitable
sections.text:
Suppose the same 100 shares could be sold at KES 21. Gross sale value would be KES 2,100. Under an invented 2% sale charge, the sale cost is KES 42 and proceeds are KES 2,058. Comparing KES 2,058 with the KES 2,040 purchase outlay leaves KES 18 before any omitted tax or other cost. The price rose by KES 1 per share, but the investor did not retain the full KES 100 gross difference.

If the sale price were KES 20, net proceeds under these assumptions would be KES 1,960, producing a KES 80 loss against the KES 2,040 outlay. A price that returns to the purchase quotation therefore does not necessarily return the investor to break-even. Keep a ledger with separate columns for quantity, price, gross amount, individual charges and final cash movement. That structure makes it easier to identify an error than a single unexplained “profit” field. It also helps distinguish a price change from the amount actually retained.

sections.heading: Calculate a break-even price under explicit assumptions
sections.text:
For a percentage-only example, write purchase outlay as quantity times purchase price times one plus the buy-fee rate. Write net sale proceeds as quantity times sale price times one minus the sell-fee rate. Setting those two expressions equal gives the sale price needed to break even under that model. With a KES 20 purchase and 2% on each side, the result is 20 times 1.02 divided by 0.98, approximately KES 20.8163 per share.

The number is useful only with its assumptions attached. A fixed charge or minimum fee changes the equation, and rounding can matter when reconciling an actual statement. A calculated price also does not guarantee that a buyer will be available at that price. The fee calculator uses this percentage-only model to make one relationship visible. It does not establish a target price, account for every tax treatment or promise an executable trade. Use the calculation to ask better questions about the provider's actual tariff and the market conditions.

sections.heading: Minimum and repeated costs can change a comparison
sections.text:
A fixed or minimum charge can matter more to a small transaction than to a larger one. In a fictional tariff, a KES 50 fixed charge represents 5% of a KES 1,000 trade but 0.5% of a KES 10,000 trade. This arithmetic does not mean that a person should increase an order beyond an appropriate amount merely to reduce a percentage. It means that a headline percentage alone can fail to describe the economic effect of a tariff.

Frequency matters too. If a hypothetical round trip costs KES 80, repeating it ten times consumes KES 800 before considering gains or losses. A series of small gross wins may therefore leave little after costs. Compare a strategy's activity level with the costs it generates rather than looking at one selected winning trade. Ask which costs recur, which depend on size, and which apply even when an order does not lead to the hoped-for result. Keep the assumptions consistent across comparisons so that changing the tariff is not confused with changing the trading outcome.

sections.heading: Price spreads and execution belong beside the tariff
sections.text:
Some economic costs do not appear as a simple line labelled commission. If the best available buying interest and selling interest differ, an immediate buy followed by an immediate sale can lose value even before explicit charges. A moving market or limited quantity at a quoted price can also produce a different execution from the one assumed. These effects should not be merged carelessly with the provider's published fees: label what you know, what you estimated and what occurred.

In your practice notes, maintain a gross result and a net result under a stated cost model. When actual records are available, reconcile them instead of silently replacing them with an estimate. Explain why the classroom's zero-fee, fixed-price simulator cannot test a strategy's real profitability. An honest comparison can end with “more information required” if you do not have a complete tariff or reliable execution assumptions. Knowing how to calculate costs is valuable; knowing when the calculation is incomplete is equally necessary for making sense of it.

example.title: A fictional round trip
example.text:
Buy 100 shares at KES 20: the shares cost KES 2,000. Suppose a teaching fee is 2% on each side. Purchase outlay is KES 2,040. Sell at KES 21: gross value is KES 2,100 and net proceeds are KES 2,058. Net gain is KES 18, not KES 100. These are invented fees, excluding tax.

Test the fee model with an unchanged sale price. A hundred shares bought at KES 20 with an invented two-percent buy charge require KES 2,040. Selling those shares at KES 20 with the same assumed percentage sale charge returns KES 1,960. The loss is KES 80, even though the quoted price is unchanged. Now replace the percentage-only assumption with a hypothetical fixed KES 50 charge on a KES 1,000 transaction. That charge is five percent of the gross trade amount. Do not combine the two examples unless the imagined tariff explicitly includes both items. Write down which fee applies on which side and which base it uses. Finally, explain why a break-even calculation does not create a willing counterparty or guarantee execution. This worksheet should expose assumptions clearly enough that a different learner could replace them with a documented tariff.

lessons.summary: Understand income, price changes and the difference between gross and net.
outcomes: Calculate a simple dividend yield
Calculate a holding-period return
Recognise why a high yield can be misleading

sections.heading: Income is not the whole return
sections.text: A dividend is a distribution declared by a company. It is not a fixed salary for owning shares. Payment amounts and eligibility depend on the company announcement; use official dates and records.

sections.heading: Keep the denominator clear
sections.text: A simple dividend yield divides annual dividend per share by share price. A yield on your historical purchase price is a different measure. Comparing percentages with different denominators can mislead you.

sections.heading: Combine income and price change
sections.text: A holding-period return can include dividends and a price gain or loss. For a realistic net result, account for transaction costs and applicable taxes. A large headline yield can accompany a falling share price.

sections.heading: Follow the declaration and entitlement, not an assumption
sections.text:
A dividend begins with a company decision under the applicable rules and its circumstances. Do not assume that a past payment creates a promise of another payment of the same size. Profit, cash needs, financing commitments and other considerations can affect a distribution. Read the actual announcement for what is declared, who is entitled and the relevant dates. Procedures and dates must be checked for the specific security and market rather than borrowed from a general overseas example.

Buying immediately before a payment is not automatically a way to obtain free money. The price can change, entitlement depends on the applicable arrangements, and charges or tax can affect the amount retained. Keep the company announcement, the account record and the cash actually received as separate evidence. A video describing an annual payout does not prove that you personally qualify for it. In a research note, distinguish a proposed distribution, a declared amount and a payment already received. That simple separation prevents several common mistakes in dividend discussions.

sections.heading: Yield is a ratio with a changing denominator
sections.text:
Dividend yield compares a stated annual dividend per share with a stated share price. If an assumed annual dividend is KES 2 and the price is KES 50, the gross yield is 2 divided by 50, or 4%. If the price falls to KES 25 while the assumed dividend stays at KES 2, the calculated yield becomes 8%. The higher percentage does not by itself show that the business has improved. It may reflect a lower price, a stale dividend assumption or a greater perceived risk.

Always identify the numerator and denominator. Is the dividend historical, declared or merely expected? Is the price today's quotation, your own purchase price or an average cost? Different choices answer different questions. Two people can report different yields for the same security without using the same calculation basis. Keep the basis beside the percentage rather than treating yield as a fixed property printed permanently on a share. Then investigate whether the assumptions are appropriate before making any comparison with another investment or another source of income.

sections.heading: Separate gross income from what reaches the account
sections.text:
A headline dividend per share is not necessarily the amount you retain. Relevant tax treatment, account arrangements and any applicable charges need current information for the actual investor and transaction. A classroom example can calculate gross income without claiming to establish those rules. With 200 shares and an invented KES 1.50 dividend per share, gross income would be KES 300. Label it gross, and reconcile the actual account credit separately when dealing with a real payment.

Do not quietly change a before-tax example into an after-tax claim in a comparison. Likewise, do not compare a gross dividend yield with another product's net return without explaining the difference. Ask whether the figures cover the same period, currency, reinvestment assumption and costs. These questions do not tell you which product to choose. They help prevent a calculation from appearing more precise or comparable than it really is. A reliable worksheet shows the starting figures, the assumptions, the formula and the items that have not yet been established.

sections.heading: Measure the whole holding-period result
sections.text:
For a simple period with no extra purchases or sales, combine the change in value with cash distributions, then account for costs and tax as relevant. Imagine buying 100 shares at KES 40, receiving KES 200 of gross dividends and later selling at KES 37. The price loss is KES 300 and the gross dividend is KES 200, leaving a KES 100 loss before costs and tax. The existence of income does not guarantee a positive total result.

Use a cash ledger if the sequence is more complicated. Record the purchase outlay, later contributions, distributions, sales and final remaining value. A return calculation can be distorted if fresh deposits are mistaken for investment gains. A simple holding-period percentage is useful for a clearly defined single investment; multiple cash flows may require a different method. Do not annualise a short unusually favourable period and present it as an expected yearly outcome. State the dates and calculation method so another learner can reproduce what you measured.

sections.heading: Ask whether the distribution fits the business
sections.text:
A distribution can be considered alongside earnings, operating cash flow, investment needs and financing. A company may report a profit while collecting cash slowly, or it may need cash to maintain and develop its operations. Look for the explanation in the reports rather than assuming that a large payout is always evidence of strength. A dividend funded in a particular way can have different implications from one supported by recurring cash generation. Context matters more than an isolated percentage.

Create two fictional cases with the same reported dividend yield. In one, earnings and cash generation are stable and the company explains its investment needs. In the other, a major customer has left and the dividend estimate comes from last year's announcement. The same ratio hides different questions. Your task is not to guess a future payment with certainty. It is to identify the evidence supporting the assumption, the circumstances that could change it and how a change would affect the reason you were considering the investment.

example.title: A positive dividend, negative total result
example.text:
You buy one imaginary share for KES 50, receive KES 2 in dividends, then sell for KES 45. Ignoring costs and tax, the total result is 45 + 2 − 50 = −KES 3, or −6%. Receiving a dividend did not prevent a loss.

Use a complete fictional holding period. A learner buys a hundred shares at KES 40, receives a KES 2-per-share gross distribution and later sells at KES 37. Purchase value is KES 4,000, gross dividend income is KES 200 and sale value is KES 3,700. The combined amount is KES 3,900, a KES 100 loss before costs and tax. A five-percent dividend-on-purchase-price calculation is therefore not the same as a five-percent total return. Ask the learner to label the dates, the dividend assumption and the sale assumption. Then replace the sale price with KES 42 and recompute rather than changing the verbal explanation alone. The exercise shows how the components connect. It does not imply that either price or dividend is a forecast, or that the same distribution will be repeated in a later period.

lessons.title: Compounding & realistic expectations
lessons.summary: Explore growth mathematics without confusing it with a forecast.
outcomes: Explain returns on earlier returns
See the effect of regular contributions
Recognise the limits of fixed-rate examples

sections.heading: What compounding means
sections.text: When earnings remain invested, later returns can apply to a larger amount. Adding new savings is a separate contribution; it is not investment profit. Keep those two sources of growth distinct.

sections.heading: Use a scenario, not a prediction
sections.text: A fixed annual rate is a convenient teaching assumption. Share returns vary and can be negative. Reinvesting dividends does not remove market risk, fees, taxes or the possibility of losing money.

sections.heading: Time does not erase a bad decision
sections.text: A long horizon may allow more time to respond to setbacks, but a failing business can still lose value permanently. Review your assumptions rather than treating every investment as certain to recover.

sections.heading: A return applies to the balance that actually exists
sections.text:
Compounding means that a later period's return applies to an amount that includes earlier results. With an invented KES 1,000 starting amount and a constant 5% yearly return, the first year ends at KES 1,050. Applying 5% to KES 1,050 produces KES 1,102.50 after the second year. The additional KES 2.50 relative to simple interest comes from earning a return on the first year's result. The calculation is exact under those assumptions; the assumptions are not a promise about shares.

Losses also compound. A sequence of a 10% increase and a 10% decrease produces 1.10 times 0.90, or 0.99 of the starting amount, before costs. You do not return to the starting balance just because the two percentages have opposite signs. Use multiplication period by period rather than simply adding returns. This habit is useful both for checking a calculator and for questioning an attractive performance presentation. Ask what happened to the amount actually present at each stage, not only which average percentage looks most impressive.

sections.heading: Contributions are your money, not an investment gain
sections.text:
If you add KES 1,000 every month for twelve months, you have contributed KES 12,000. That fact must be separated from any return the investment earns. An account that grows because of deposits has not necessarily generated an investment profit of the same size. A useful scenario report displays contributions, ending value and the difference between them. When comparing two plans, keep the contribution amounts and dates consistent so that one is not favoured simply because more money was added.

Timing changes the arithmetic. A contribution made at the start of a period can earn that period's assumed return; one made at the end cannot. Our growth tool adds monthly contributions at month-end and converts an assumed effective annual rate into its equivalent constant monthly rate. It uses a smooth invented path. Real prices do not follow that path. Before sharing a calculator result, write down both the contribution timing and the rate convention. Those details help another person understand the calculation instead of mistaking it for a prediction.

sections.heading: Compare several paths instead of choosing one exciting rate
sections.text:
A model is more useful when you test its sensitivity. Keep the starting amount and contributions fixed, then compare a lower, a middle and a negative-return assumption. Ask how much of the ending balance comes from saving rather than the chosen return. A very high rate can create a large displayed number without making the underlying outcome likely. The right response to that sensitivity is to examine the assumption, not to treat the largest number as a target that the market owes you.

For a simple two-year lump sum of KES 10,000, constant annual assumptions of 0%, 5% and minus 5% produce KES 10,000, KES 11,025 and KES 9,025 before costs. These are mathematical scenarios. They do not define a probability distribution or a forecast. A real sequence can include substantial fluctuations within those years, and you may need money during a decline. Explain what the model leaves out, including fees, taxes, inflation and changing contributions, before using its output in a personal plan.

sections.heading: Purchasing power and nominal cash are different measures
sections.text:
An ending amount measured in shillings is a nominal figure. What that amount can buy depends on the prices of the goods and services relevant to the goal. In a fictional one-year example, an investment grows by 8% while the chosen measure of prices rises by 6%. Comparing 1.08 with 1.06 gives a real change of approximately 1.9%, rather than 8%. These invented rates illustrate the difference; they are not a report of current Kenyan inflation or a suggested return assumption.

The appropriate inflation question depends on the goal and period. School costs, housing costs and a broad price index need not move identically. Avoid solving that uncertainty by inventing a single precise number. Instead, document the measure and assumptions used and explore what different costs would do to the plan. A nominal gain can coexist with reduced purchasing power, just as a rising account balance can partly reflect new deposits. Good financial explanations identify what is being measured before celebrating an increase.

sections.heading: Judge the method by its transparency, not its confidence
sections.text:
When someone presents a future value, request the starting amount, contribution schedule, time period, return convention and treatment of costs. Ask whether distributions are reinvested and whether the figures are before or after tax and inflation. If those details are missing, the final number cannot be properly checked. A neat chart is not a replacement for the assumptions that generated it. An honest explanation can show a range of possible scenarios without pretending to know which will occur.

Use this classroom tool as an experiment. Enter a simple case you can calculate by hand, such as a zero-return case with regular contributions. Then change one input and explain why the output changes. Finally, write one sentence naming a real-world feature the tool does not model. This approach builds understanding without encouraging the belief that a calculator can remove uncertainty. Time and disciplined saving can matter greatly to a plan, but neither a long time horizon nor a compounding formula guarantees a profitable outcome from a particular share or strategy.

example.title: Two invented years
example.text:
Start with KES 10,000 and assume 5% growth each year, with no new contributions or costs. The first year ends at KES 10,500. The second ends at KES 11,025. The second year’s KES 525 is larger because its starting amount is larger. A real share portfolio will not follow this smooth path.

Check a small scenario without a complicated calculator. Begin with an imaginary KES 1,000 and no extra contributions. At a constant five-percent annual assumption, the first year adds KES 50 and the second adds KES 52.50, ending at KES 1,102.50. Next use a zero-return assumption and add KES 100 at each of twelve month-ends. Contributions add KES 1,200, so the ending amount is KES 2,200. The increase is entirely new saving in this second example, not investment profit. Write the rate convention and timing beside each case. A scenario with a variable market path, different contribution dates, costs or inflation would require different calculations. The value of this exercise is that you can explain why the number changes and identify which real-world features are absent, rather than assuming the tool has predicted the amount you will eventually receive.

lessons.title: Read a company before its chart
lessons.summary: Use financial statements to ask better questions about a business.
outcomes: Identify the three main statements
Separate accounting profit from cash
Find questions worth investigating

sections.heading: Start with how the business earns
sections.text: Describe the customer, product and major costs. Then open the latest annual report and results from the company or an official issuer source. Record the reporting period before comparing numbers.

sections.heading: Three lenses on the same business
sections.text: An income statement shows performance over a period. A balance sheet is a snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity. A cash-flow statement tracks cash movements. Read them together rather than treating one number as a complete verdict.

sections.heading: Follow the questions
sections.text: Check whether reported growth is recurring, whether debt can be serviced, and whether operating cash supports profits. Read the notes and auditor’s report. Unfamiliar terms are a reason to investigate, not to guess.

sections.heading: Start with the business model and the reporting period
sections.text:
Before calculating a ratio, explain how the company earns revenue, what it must spend and which resources it needs. A retailer, a lender and a manufacturer have different operating structures. A number that is sensible to compare within one business may be misleading across unrelated businesses. Identify the reporting period, currency and units before copying figures. A statement in millions of shillings should not be combined casually with a share count or debt figure expressed in another unit.

Find the company's own report and read the explanatory notes around the figures you use. Check whether the result covers a full year or an interim period and whether comparative figures have been restated. A headline can omit a change in accounting presentation or a major one-off event. Record both the number and its definition. Your first research page should allow another learner to locate the original figure and understand why you think it is relevant, rather than merely repeating an impressive percentage from a summary.

sections.heading: Use the income statement to ask how the result was produced
sections.text:
An income statement describes financial performance over a period. Revenue, expenses and profit are connected but different quantities. Growth in sales is not the same thing as growth in profit, and profit growth can come from factors other than stronger ordinary operations. Look for changes in costs, financing expenses and unusual gains or losses. Compare a trend across relevant periods instead of treating one favourable year as a complete picture of a business.

For a fictional seller with KES 1 million of revenue and KES 700,000 of direct costs, the gross difference is KES 300,000 before other operating expenses, finance costs and tax. Calling that amount final net profit would skip important items. If revenue rises while costs rise faster, a larger business can produce a weaker margin. Write a short bridge explaining what changed rather than relying on a single growth rate. The aim is to understand the result's composition and sustainability, not to find a ratio that automatically says “buy.”

sections.heading: Read the balance sheet as a dated position
sections.text:
The balance sheet relates assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time. In a simplified example, assets of KES 12 million and liabilities of KES 7 million leave equity of KES 5 million. The equation balances, but it does not by itself establish the market value of the shares or the quality of every asset. Ask what the assets consist of, when obligations fall due and whether important estimates or commitments require further reading.

Two companies can have the same total assets but very different flexibility. One may hold accessible cash and readily collected receivables; another may have specialised equipment or inventory that is difficult to realise quickly. Debt maturity and financing conditions can also matter when assessing resilience. A balance sheet is a starting map, not a guarantee that every recorded amount can be turned into cash at that value immediately. Use the notes and other statements to understand the resources and obligations behind the totals.

sections.heading: Profit and cash flow tell related stories
sections.text:
Accounting can recognise activity before the related cash is collected or paid. A fictional company may make a credit sale and record revenue while the customer has not yet settled the invoice. That can support reported profit without producing the same-period cash inflow. Non-cash expenses and movements in working capital create further differences. Neither statement should be dismissed merely because it differs from the other; investigate how the accounts connect.

Read the cash-flow categories and the company's explanations for major movements. Consider cash generated by operations alongside investment in assets and cash raised from or returned to finance providers. A positive total cash movement funded by new borrowing is different from cash generated by recurring operations. Conversely, investment spending can reduce current cash while supporting a project whose outcome still needs evaluation. Avoid shortcuts such as “cash rose, therefore the business improved.” Explain the source and use of the cash, and identify what is recurring, uncertain or dependent on financing.

sections.heading: Turn a report into a question-led research note
sections.text:
Choose a few questions that fit the business. Are customers paying on time? What explains a change in margin? How is an expansion financed? Which assumptions support an asset value? What would put pressure on the company's ability to meet obligations? Find the relevant disclosures, record their dates and note the limits of the information. A company's own narrative is useful evidence of management's explanation, but it should not be treated as independent proof that every expectation will be achieved.

Prepare a one-page note with a business description, three sourced figures, a connection between two statements, and a question the report does not fully answer. Separate your interpretation from the company's statement. If you cannot explain an important item, keep it unresolved rather than filling the gap with a price-chart story. This is the foundation for valuation: understanding the business and the quality of its information comes before deciding what a share might be worth. A clear decision to investigate further can be a stronger result than a confident conclusion built on misunderstood figures.

example.text:
An imaginary wholesaler sells KES 1 million of goods on credit. It may report revenue before all customers pay. Ask how much cash was actually collected, what customers still owe, and whether those amounts are recoverable.

Construct a fictional three-statement question. A company reports a KES 100,000 credit sale that has not yet been collected. The sale can contribute to recorded revenue while the cash collection remains outstanding; the accounting details depend on the transaction and reporting rules. Ask what the receivable represents, when payment is expected and which expenses also affect the result. Then identify the period and units of every figure. The exercise should produce connections and questions, not a stock pick. If you cannot explain an important item in a real report, mark it for further investigation rather than filling the gap with a favourable price chart.

lessons.title: Valuation: price is not value
lessons.summary: Use simple ratios as questions, rather than automatic stock picks.
outcomes: Calculate earnings per share and P/E
Distinguish share price from company size
Recognise limitations of ratio comparisons

sections.heading: One share’s price says little by itself
sections.text: Two companies can have very different numbers of shares outstanding. Multiplying price by shares gives a market capitalisation. A KES 5 share is not automatically cheaper in valuation terms than a KES 100 share.

sections.heading: Know what a ratio contains
sections.text: In a simplified example, earnings per share is profit attributable to ordinary shareholders divided by ordinary shares. A P/E ratio divides price by earnings per share. Real reporting may include diluted shares and adjustments, so use the report’s definitions.

sections.heading: Ask why the numbers differ
sections.text: A low P/E may reflect weak prospects, unusual earnings or concern about the business. A high one may reflect optimistic expectations that fail to materialise. Compare like periods and similar businesses, and avoid using P/E when earnings are negative as if it were an ordinary positive multiple.

sections.heading: A share price is not the price of the whole business
sections.text:
Compare a fictional Company A with one million shares at KES 10 and Company B with ten million shares at KES 2. Their equity market values are KES 10 million and KES 20 million respectively. B has a lower price per share but a larger total equity valuation under these assumptions. The number of units matters. Share splits, new issues and different share classes can complicate a comparison further, so identify the relevant share count and rights.

Equity value also differs from the value attributed to the whole operating business in some valuation methods. Financing claims, debt, cash and other adjustments can matter when moving between enterprise and equity measures. Do not mix a whole-business numerator with an equity-only denominator without understanding the method. A beginner can start by labelling each quantity correctly and checking units. The goal is not to memorise a complicated formula first; it is to avoid treating a small quoted unit price as evidence that a security is inexpensive.

sections.heading: Read a multiple as a question about its inputs
sections.text:
The price-to-earnings ratio compares share price with a defined earnings-per-share figure. An invented KES 4 price and KES 0.50 of annual earnings per share give a P/E of eight. That arithmetic is straightforward. The interpretation is harder: which period's earnings are used, were there unusual items, how stable is the business, and what financing or accounting choices affected the result? A low ratio can reflect concerns about future earnings rather than an overlooked bargain.

Negative or very small earnings can make a simple P/E comparison particularly unhelpful. An unusually strong year in a cyclical business can also make the ratio look low just when the earnings base is difficult to repeat. Compare relevant businesses and periods, but do not assume their differences disappear because they share a sector label. Write what the multiple might be signalling and what else you would need to check. A ratio is a compressed description of chosen inputs, not an instruction to trade.

sections.heading: Distinguish a useful company from an attractive price
sections.text:
A business can have desirable products, capable staff and growing demand while its shares are priced on demanding expectations. If those expectations are not achieved, an investor may experience a poor return even though the business continues to operate successfully. The reverse question is also important: a troubled business can look statistically cheap without offering a convincing way to improve. Quality and price need to be considered together rather than treated as interchangeable labels.

Imagine two possible futures for the same fictional company. One assumes that growth continues and costs remain controlled. Another assumes a major customer leaves and financing becomes more expensive. Explain how those different futures affect the case rather than selecting the more pleasant one as a certainty. Identify the evidence supporting each assumption and the information that would change your view. You do not need to turn every uncertainty into an exact probability to learn from a scenario comparison. You do need to show which expectations your conclusion depends on.

sections.heading: Present value makes assumptions visible
sections.text:
A present-value model relates future cash amounts to a value today using a stated discount rate and timing convention. For an invented KES 100 received one year from now and an assumed 10% rate, the present value is 100 divided by 1.10, approximately KES 90.91. This is a mathematical relationship under the assumptions, not a guaranteed price at which anyone will trade an asset. Uncertain cash flows require careful thought about both the forecasts and the valuation method.

Changing the rate or the cash forecast changes the result. A highly detailed spreadsheet can therefore look precise while remaining sensitive to a few uncertain choices. Keep the assumptions visible and examine alternatives. Do not substitute a convenient rate simply to produce the value you wanted. For a beginner, the most important lesson is that a value estimate is conditional. A later update can be justified by new evidence, but changing assumptions only because the market price moved does not automatically improve the original reasoning.

sections.heading: Write a valuation range with a case against yourself
sections.text:
Create a short valuation note that identifies the method, inputs, dates, units and limits. Include an alternative case that challenges your preferred interpretation. Ask whether a reported result is recurring, whether financing adds vulnerability and whether information is missing. A range of defensible assumptions can be more honest than one unsupported exact number. It still is not a promise about the next market quotation or the timing of a possible return.

Finish by describing what would make you wait. Examples include an unexplained accounting item, a missing report, unclear debt terms or a result that depends on exceptionally optimistic growth. These are prompts for investigation, not automatic rejection rules for every investor. Compare the valuation question with your intended horizon and the costs of acting. If you cannot explain how the evidence connects to the price being considered, keep the exercise as research. Confidence should come from a transparent process that can be challenged, not from the number of decimal places in a spreadsheet.

example.title: A deliberately simple P/E
example.text:
A fictional company earns KES 20 million and has 10 million ordinary shares. Simplified earnings per share is KES 2. At a price of KES 30, its P/E is 15. That calculation alone does not tell you whether the shares are suitable.

Compare two invented equity valuations. One million shares at KES 10 imply KES 10 million of market equity value. Ten million shares at KES 2 imply KES 20 million. The lower unit price belongs to the larger total equity valuation. If a different fictional company has KES 0.50 of annual earnings per share and trades at KES 4, its simple P/E is eight, provided those inputs are the ones intended. You still need to examine the earnings period, unusual items, debt and business context. Now ask what happens to the interpretation if the earnings are not repeatable. Do not change the ratio into a command to buy. Write one reason the price might be justified, one reason the case could be weak and one source you would check next. A transparent comparison preserves uncertainty while making the arithmetic reproducible.
