lessons.title: Shares, bonds, funds & diversification
lessons.summary: Compare basic product structures and look for overlapping risks.
outcomes: Distinguish equity from debt
Understand pooled investments
Check concentration across holdings

sections.heading: Ownership and lending differ
sections.text: Shares represent ownership. Bonds generally represent debt with specified contractual terms. Bondholders face risks too, including issuer default and changes in market value; the word “bond” does not make an investment risk-free.

sections.heading: Understand the wrapper
sections.text: Funds pool investors’ money. An ETF trades on an exchange, while a REIT provides a structure for property-related investment. Read the product documents to learn what it holds, how it is priced, how you can exit and what it charges. Check local approval and availability.

sections.heading: Count risks, not just tickers
sections.text: Several holdings can still depend on the same sector or economic driver. Review what a fund owns before assuming it adds something different to your portfolio. The classroom’s four-company sample is a mechanics exercise, not a diversified investment model.

sections.heading: Ownership, lending and pooled exposure create different claims
sections.text:
A share represents ownership in a company. A bond generally represents lending under contractual terms. A fund pools money under a stated investment structure and policy. These broad descriptions help organise the first questions, but they do not settle every product's risk or access conditions. Read the actual instrument documents for its rights, cash flows, charges and restrictions. Products with similar names can differ substantially in what they hold and how an investor can enter or exit.

For a fictional comparison, write who owes or owns what, what payments may occur, and what happens if the underlying issuer or assets perform poorly. Do not assume that a contractual coupon eliminates default risk, or that a fund label means broad diversification. The classroom's direct-share simulator does not represent all these instruments. Use the product comparison to understand the differences before drawing conclusions about suitability. Confirm current Kenyan availability, provider authorisation and terms through official and product-specific sources rather than applying an overseas example without checking.

sections.heading: A bond's cash flows do not make its price immovable
sections.text:
A conventional fixed-coupon bond can have specified payment and repayment terms, subject to the issuer meeting its obligations. If market-required returns change, the price someone is willing to pay for those fixed cash flows can change as well. All else equal, higher required yields tend to reduce the value of an existing stream of fixed payments. Credit concerns, remaining term and other features can also affect value. A promised schedule and a guaranteed market resale price are different ideas.

An investor who needs to sell before maturity should investigate the market and exit conditions rather than assuming the original purchase amount will be available. Even holding to maturity does not remove the need to understand issuer risk, the actual contract and the effect of inflation. These general principles are not a statement of a specific bond's current yield, tax treatment or eligibility. Obtain the terms for the real instrument and keep the comparison consistent with the time when the money might be needed.

sections.heading: Look through a fund to its holdings and structure
sections.text:
A pooled investment may spread exposure across many securities, but the mandate determines what it can hold. A narrowly focused fund can remain concentrated in one sector, country or style. A fund's largest holdings may overlap with securities you own directly or with another fund. Read the investment policy, holdings information and risk disclosures rather than counting fund names as separate independent exposures.

Also understand how units are bought, valued and redeemed or traded. An exchange-traded instrument can involve market prices and trading liquidity, while another structure may use different subscription or redemption arrangements. Fees, tracking differences, exit conditions and operational details belong in the comparison. A product's marketing phrase does not explain all those features. This lesson does not recommend an index, fund or account. It teaches you to identify the actual assets, rights, costs and processes that sit beneath a product label.

sections.heading: Diversification is about underlying dependence
sections.text:
Consider two imaginary portfolios with ten account lines each. The first depends heavily on one industry and one customer group. The second has a wider spread of economic exposures. Both contain ten names, but the number alone does not tell you which risks dominate. Correlations can also change under stressed conditions, so a tidy historical pattern is not a promise that holdings will offset one another in every future period.

Map the reasons each holding might be affected by an event. Interest rates, commodity prices, customer demand, currency movements and financing access can connect apparently different businesses. Then ask whether the total arrangement fits the stated goal and need for liquidity. Diversification can reduce particular concentrations without eliminating market risk or guaranteeing a positive result. Avoid presenting it as a magic number of shares. A useful explanation identifies the exposure being reduced, the costs and limitations of the change, and the risks that remain.

sections.heading: Make a comparison table before chasing a headline yield
sections.text:
Use the same headings for each product: what it represents, the source of potential return, possible loss mechanisms, access to money, costs, information available and provider arrangements. Label figures as historical, current or assumed. Compare like periods and like calculation bases, including whether distributions are reinvested and whether costs are included. A large percentage printed on an advert is not a complete description of the product or its likely outcome.

End the table with unanswered questions rather than a forced winner. You may discover that you do not yet understand a redemption restriction, a concentration or an account structure. That is useful progress. Revisit the relevant official sources or seek a suitable explanation before applying the comparison to real money. The aim of learning about several instruments is to widen your judgement and vocabulary, not to make every new product look necessary. A deliberate decision to keep researching can be more appropriate than adding complexity simply because a product is unfamiliar or fashionable.

example.title: Three labels, one exposure
example.text:
Imagine owning Bank A shares, Bank B shares and units in a fund invested mostly in those same banks. You have three holdings, but the banking sector remains a shared source of risk.

Design a three-column comparison for a fictional share, bond and fund. For the share, describe ownership and uncertain distributions and resale value. For the conventional bond, distinguish contractual payments from issuer risk and a changing resale price. For the fund, identify the underlying assets and entry or exit arrangements instead of assuming that the label means broad diversification. Use matching time periods and make costs visible. Then imagine owning three funds that all have a large exposure to the same industry. There are three account lines but an important shared dependency. Explain what additional holdings information would be needed before describing the arrangement as well diversified. The exercise does not rank the products or claim any current Kenyan availability. Its purpose is to turn product names into a set of understandable claims, risks, processes and unanswered questions.

lessons.summary: Turn what you have learned into a repeatable decision process.
outcomes: Identify pressure and guaranteed-return claims
Verify information independently
Write a simple plan before investing

sections.heading: Slow down when someone rushes you
sections.text: Guaranteed high returns, pressure to transfer immediately and unverifiable success stories deserve scrutiny. A convincing website or a paid endorsement is not proof that an offer is legitimate.

sections.heading: Verify using a different route
sections.text: Find the provider through official sources rather than relying on a link in an unsolicited message. Check the legal entity, licence category and contact details. Never share passwords or one-time codes with someone offering to “help” you invest.

sections.heading: Write down your own decision rules
sections.text: Describe your goal, timeframe, savings capacity and the losses you can afford. Decide what evidence you need, how you will review the investment, and what would change your view. Keep records and learn the provider’s complaint process.

sections.heading: Pause when urgency replaces a verifiable explanation
sections.text:
An offer can use excitement, authority claims and social proof to discourage questions. High-return promises combined with pressure to pay immediately are a strong reason to pause. Ask what economic activity could produce the claimed return, what losses are possible, who is responsible for the arrangement and which independent records support the story. A payment screenshot or a testimonial does not establish that an investment is legitimate or sustainable.

Do not confuse a demand for proof with a promise that every genuine investment will be easy to understand. Legitimate products can be complex and can lose money. The difference is that uncertainty and terms should be investigated rather than hidden behind urgency. A word such as guaranteed requires a credible explanation of the actual obligation and backing; it is not a substitute for either. If the person presenting the offer refuses reasonable verification or says that asking questions will make you miss out, record that behaviour as part of the evidence.

sections.heading: Verify identities through a route the promoter does not control
sections.text:
Search the exact legal name in the appropriate official register and compare the listed category with the service offered. Use independently found contact details to check a claimed affiliation. A cloned website, copied logo or genuine registration number can be attached to an unrelated request. Do not let a link supplied by the promoter be your only route to confirming the promoter's identity.

Keep a record of what you checked and when. If the legal entity, service, website and payment instructions do not fit together, stop and seek clarification through a verified channel. Registration or licensing is not a guarantee of a profitable investment, but failing to establish the identity of the counterparty leaves an even more basic question unresolved. Avoid transferring funds to prove that you are serious or sharing authentication details so that someone can “activate” an opportunity. Those requests are not evidence about the underlying investment.

sections.heading: Examine the process behind a performance claim
sections.text:
A selected winning trade tells you little about a complete history. Ask whether the presentation includes losses, unsuccessful attempts, costs, the time period and the amount exposed. An attractive percentage can describe a small selected position while omitting the rest of an account. An account balance can also include new deposits. The relevant question is how the claimed result was calculated and what independent evidence is available, not simply whether the picture looks professional.

Be careful about interpreting lucky outcomes as proof of a repeatable method. A strategy can take substantial hidden risk and still look successful for a while. Likewise, a losing decision does not by itself prove that every part of the reasoning was careless. The journal and later discipline classes separate process from outcome. Apply that distinction to other people's claims too. An explanation that admits limits and allows checking is more useful for learning than a confident promise that asks you to suspend examination.

sections.heading: A first plan should include reasons to do nothing
sections.text:
Write a plan before choosing a security. Describe the goal, intended horizon, information needed, costs to investigate and circumstances that would make you wait. Include how you will record decisions and when you will review the plan. Do not turn another person's preferred percentage allocation or daily trading routine into a personal rule without considering the context. This classroom provides exercises and questions; it does not assess what exposure you personally can afford.

For a practice idea, require a business explanation, a dated source, a cost assumption and a reason the idea could fail. If any item is missing, use the gap as a research task. A plan can be short while still being specific. “Buy something that will rise” is not a reviewable plan because it does not explain the evidence, alternatives or conditions. “Investigate further because the account structure and fees are unclear” is a concrete decision that can protect the quality of the process without pretending to predict the market.

sections.heading: Keep evidence and use the appropriate help route
sections.text:
If you encounter a suspicious request or an unresolved account issue, preserve the relevant messages, dates, transaction references and documents. Do not publish sensitive identity details or passwords in an attempt to get help quickly. Use the provider's verified support route and the relevant official reporting or complaint process for the circumstances. Read the current procedure rather than assuming every concern follows the same sequence or falls under the same institution.

Be especially cautious about a second unsolicited offer that promises to recover a loss for an advance payment or requests fresh access credentials. A difficult earlier experience can make urgency more persuasive. Return to the same habits of independent identity checks and careful documentation. Learning to recognise a concern does not require you to prove a legal case or to confront a suspected promoter yourself. A useful classroom outcome is to identify what is known, preserve the evidence appropriately, stop further exposure where necessary and locate the legitimate channel for advice or assistance.

example.title: A warning-sign exercise
example.text:
A stranger promises to double your money in seven days and says the last place is available only if you pay now. There is no need to prove exactly how the scheme works before declining. Pause, preserve the message, and verify independently.

Review a fictional message that offers unusually high regular returns, claims an official partnership and asks for immediate payment. The first task is to pause and establish the identity and service through independent channels. A logo, copied registration number or selected profit screenshot does not complete that check. Next ask how the stated return is produced, what losses are possible and what records support the story. If the promoter refuses the questions, record that response rather than treating urgency as evidence. Build a practice plan with a clear no-action condition, such as not proceeding while the legal entity or charges remain unverified. Finally, name the legitimate support or reporting channel you would consult and the documents you would preserve. You do not need to prove every allegation to recognise that an important verification step is missing.

lessons.title: Investor or trader: choose a process
lessons.summary: Understand different decision horizons before choosing a strategy.
outcomes: Separate a business thesis from a trading hypothesis
Account for the demands of frequent decisions
Recognise that choosing not to trade is valid

sections.heading: Two different questions
sections.text: An investor might ask how a business could produce value over several years. A trader might test a shorter-term hypothesis about price and execution. Neither label guarantees skill or profit.

sections.heading: Match the process to the resources
sections.text: A shorter horizon can demand more monitoring, more decisions and more trading costs. Consider time, available data, liquidity and emotional demands before copying someone else’s style. Do not interpret another market’s rules as Kenyan requirements.

sections.heading: Keep your original reason visible
sections.text: A trade that moves against you does not automatically become a sound long-term investment. Revisit the evidence and the original decision rules. Remaining in cash or continuing to learn can be a deliberate decision.

sections.heading: Define the horizon before selecting the evidence
sections.text:
An investment thesis might focus on a business's ability to generate cash over several years and the price paid for that claim. A trading hypothesis might concern a shorter period, a particular event or the behaviour of prices under stated conditions. These descriptions can overlap, but they require different evidence and review rules. A long business explanation does not automatically support a short price prediction, and a recent price movement does not establish the long-term value of a company.

Write the intended horizon in a sentence before opening a chart. Then explain why the evidence you propose to use is relevant to that horizon. If the original trading idea fails, do not silently rename the position a long-term investment simply to avoid acknowledging the change. A revised decision can be legitimate, but it needs its own evidence and an honest record of what changed. Keeping the original thesis visible makes it possible to review the reasoning instead of rewriting the story around the outcome.

sections.heading: Check whether the process can be carried out in the actual market
sections.text:
A hypothesis may look attractive on a chart while relying on execution conditions that are unavailable. Ask whether the relevant security can be traded in the intended size, what the spread and charges might be, which order services are supported and what information is available. Do not assume that overseas examples of leverage, short selling or automated order types describe services available to a Kenyan customer. Confirm the actual provider's terms and the relevant current rules.

Our simulator deliberately omits many of those conditions. An instant zero-fee practice trade can test whether you understand a quantity and cash movement. It cannot establish that a time-sensitive real strategy is executable or profitable. Before interpreting a practice result, list the assumptions that would need to hold outside the classroom. If the intended advantage is smaller than plausible costs or depends on a price that may not be available, the missing execution analysis is part of the hypothesis, not an inconvenient detail to leave until later.

sections.heading: Ask what would count as evidence against the idea
sections.text:
A useful hypothesis can be challenged. State the observation that would weaken it and the information that would make you stop researching or acting on it. “The price will eventually rise” has no clear review boundary and can survive almost any temporary evidence. A more useful research statement identifies the circumstances, time horizon and limits under which it is being considered. This does not guarantee that the hypothesis is correct; it makes it possible to examine it.

Separate a failed forecast from a poorly followed process. A well-documented decision can still lose because the future is uncertain. A careless decision can produce a favourable result by chance. Review both the evidence and the way the decision was implemented. Record whether the entry, costs, quantity and review conditions matched the plan. Do not use one winning outcome as permission to increase exposure automatically, or one losing outcome as proof that every underlying idea must be discarded without investigation.

sections.heading: Judge a record using all outcomes and costs
sections.text:
A strategy description needs more than its percentage of winning trades. Consider the size of gains and losses, the amount exposed, transaction costs and the period over which observations were collected. A high win rate can coexist with a negative total result if occasional losses are much larger than frequent gains. Selected examples, hypothetical fills and results without a complete cost basis cannot establish a reliable advantage.

For an invented set of ten trades, eight gains of KES 20 produce KES 160, while two losses of KES 100 remove KES 200. The result is a KES 40 loss before costs despite an 80% win rate. That arithmetic is not a forecast of any strategy. It shows why a record needs the full distribution of outcomes. A small sample also leaves substantial uncertainty about whether a pattern will persist. Treat it as material to investigate, and avoid describing a few successful practice trades as proof of professional competence.

sections.heading: Choose a learning process you can explain and review
sections.text:
Before deciding that a particular style is for you, examine the time, attention, information and emotional demands of the process. Frequent decisions can multiply costs and opportunities for error. A longer horizon does not remove valuation, financing or business risk. Neither style should be chosen because a promoter presents it as effortless income. This classroom does not determine which approach fits your circumstances; it gives you questions for evaluating the claims and requirements.

Write a learning plan with a topic to study, a source to check, a controlled practice exercise and a review date. Include a decision to wait when information is inadequate. The goal is to improve the quality of explanations before increasing complexity. If you cannot reconcile a basic order or explain an apparent return after costs, revisit those foundations before adding more sophisticated terminology. Progress is demonstrated by clearer reasoning and more accurate records, not by how frequently you act or how confidently you describe an uncertain outcome.

example.title: A changed label is not new evidence
example.text:
Imagine buying because you expected a price move within a week. After a fall, you decide to hold for five years without researching the business. The longer holding period did not create a business thesis; it changed the story you were telling yourself.

Consider a learner who enters a fictional trade expecting an event within two days. The event does not occur, and the price falls. Renaming the position a five-year investment does not automatically supply a long-term business thesis. Ask what new evidence would support a genuinely different decision and preserve the original reason in the journal. Then evaluate a separate invented record of ten trades: eight gains of KES 20 and two losses of KES 100 total a KES 40 loss before costs. Frequent wins did not establish profitability. Both parts of the exercise test whether a narrative matches the actual process and arithmetic. A capable answer can say that more research is needed, that execution assumptions are unsupported or that the small record cannot justify a claimed edge. It should not use a change in terminology to make an uncomfortable result disappear.

lessons.title: Position sizing & the limits of a stop
lessons.summary: Calculate a hypothetical exposure and understand what the calculation cannot control.
outcomes: Distinguish exposure from a planned loss budget
Calculate a simple hypothetical position size
Explain why actual losses can exceed the plan

sections.heading: Separate two amounts
sections.text: Position value is the cash committed to a holding. A planned loss budget is an amount used in a scenario. Neither determines the maximum possible loss. Treat any chosen percentage as an assumption, not a universal recommendation.

sections.heading: Make the assumptions explicit
sections.text: A simplified quantity calculation divides the planned loss budget by the assumed loss per share. Include costs in a fuller estimate and check that you can afford the position. Several positions can share the same risk.

sections.heading: Execution can change the outcome
sections.text: Where supported, a stop instruction does not guarantee the execution price. Gaps and limited liquidity can produce a worse fill; a limit condition can leave an order unfilled. Confirm the provider’s actual order facilities. This simulator has no stop orders.

sections.heading: Convert an assumed loss per share into a hypothetical size
sections.text:
A position-sizing exercise starts with explicit assumptions. Imagine a virtual account of KES 100,000, a purely illustrative loss budget of KES 1,000, an assumed entry at KES 50 and an assumed exit at KES 45. The modelled difference is KES 5 per share. Dividing KES 1,000 by KES 5 gives 200 shares before costs and other constraints. Those shares would have a gross entry value of KES 10,000. The budget is invented for arithmetic; it is not a recommended percentage for you.

Write both the amount invested and the assumed loss in the model. They are not the same quantity. Then check available cash, charges, supported quantities and other limits. If a calculation produces a fraction of a share, do not assume that the relevant service supports it. Most importantly, do not describe the result as a guaranteed maximum loss. The exercise depends on the exit occurring under the assumed conditions, which real markets and order services may not deliver.

sections.heading: A trigger does not promise a fill at the trigger price
sections.text:
A stop instruction, where supported, can use a trigger that activates another order. The trigger is not necessarily the eventual execution price. A market can move quickly, gap between available prices or have limited liquidity. A stop-limit instruction introduces a price boundary but can then fail to execute. Confirm the order types, trigger conventions and handling rules actually supported by the intermediary rather than importing assumptions from a general overseas explainer.

Return to the 200-share example. If the assumed KES 45 exit is instead executed at KES 40, the price loss from a KES 50 entry is KES 10 per share, or KES 2,000 before costs. That is twice the modelled KES 1,000 budget. If an order does not execute at all, the remaining exposure must still be understood. A sizing formula can organise thinking about a scenario, but it cannot make an uncertain execution behave like a contract guaranteeing that scenario.

sections.heading: Include costs and constraints before accepting the number
sections.text:
The gap between an assumed entry and exit is not the only potential cost. Purchase and sale charges, a spread, minimum fees and execution differences can affect the outcome. If a model uses a loss budget, explain which of those items it includes and which it leaves out. A result with several decimal places is not more reliable merely because the inputs were entered precisely. It remains conditional on the inputs and the market arrangements.

Check the gross purchase outlay against available funds and other planned obligations in the exercise. If the calculated position exceeds a cash constraint, the formula has not created extra resources. Likewise, a very narrow assumed exit difference can produce a surprisingly large position without making the idea safe. Test several adverse execution assumptions, including a much larger loss than the preferred scenario. For fully paid unlevered ordinary shares, losing the amount invested is a more severe possibility than the neat planned-exit loss; other arrangements can create additional obligations.

sections.heading: Look at the portfolio exposure, not only the new trade
sections.text:
A modest-looking new position may add to an exposure already present elsewhere. Two holdings can depend on the same business conditions, and a fund can overlap with directly owned shares. Review the total arrangement before treating each sizing calculation as independent. A collection of separate assumed loss budgets does not guarantee a limit on the portfolio's actual loss, especially when market conditions affect several holdings together.

Use a fictional account with two businesses that both depend strongly on the same customer sector. If demand in that sector weakens, the positions may decline together even though they have different names. Describe the shared exposure in words before trying to summarise it with one number. A portfolio review should also consider cash needs and the ability to exit. The purpose of this exercise is to reveal dependence and uncertainty, not to produce an allocation rule that claims to suit every learner.

sections.heading: Review the decision without chasing the calculation
sections.text:
Once a position has been sized in a hypothetical plan, record why those assumptions were selected and what would require a review. Do not repeatedly alter the assumed exit simply to make the calculated quantity larger. Do not add to a losing position only because doing so changes an average purchase price. A change in size or thesis needs a fresh explanation of evidence, available resources and downside, rather than a desire to make a previous result look better.

In the journal, compare the intended quantity, actual practice quantity, assumed costs and the conditions the simulator did not model. The classroom does not implement real stop orders or moving prices, so a successful virtual trade cannot validate a real exit plan. A useful conclusion may be that more provider information or a better understanding of execution is needed. The strongest lesson from sizing is often the boundary of the model: you can calculate a conditional exposure while still acknowledging that the actual loss may be substantially different.

example.title: An invented sizing exercise
example.text:
Assume a KES 500 planned loss budget, entry at KES 50 and an assumed exit at KES 45. Ignoring costs, 500 ÷ 5 = 100 shares, with KES 5,000 exposure. If an actual sale occurs at KES 40, the loss is KES 1,000 before costs, twice the plan. These inputs are not recommended risk limits.

Work the sizing example in both favourable and adverse execution conditions. A purely illustrative KES 1,000 modelled loss budget divided by a KES 5 assumed entry-to-exit difference gives two hundred shares. At a KES 50 entry, the gross position value is KES 10,000 before costs. If the actual hypothetical exit were KES 40 instead of KES 45, the price loss would be KES 2,000. The modelled budget is not a guarantee. Ask what happens if charges apply, an order does not execute or other holdings decline at the same time. Then explain which constraints are about available cash and which are about the uncertainty of the exit. The exercise is a way to expose conditional assumptions, not a recommended risk percentage or an instruction to create this position with real money.

lessons.title: Read price information without predicting certainty
lessons.summary: Understand charts, spreads and the limits of a visual pattern.
outcomes: Describe open, high, low and close
Distinguish a quote from a fill
Treat patterns as hypotheses

sections.heading: Read the labels first
sections.text: A chart summarises observations over a selected interval. An open, high, low and close describe that interval, not the company’s intrinsic value. Confirm the date range, data delay and whether corporate actions have been reflected.

sections.heading: Understand what a quote leaves out
sections.text: The bid is a buyer’s quoted price and the ask is a seller’s. Their difference is the spread. A quoted price and a past closing price do not guarantee the size or price at which your order can execute.

sections.heading: Keep uncertainty in the picture
sections.text: A shape on a chart is not proof of the next move. If you study a pattern, specify a rule in advance, include failed examples, and account for execution and costs. Do not select only charts that make the idea look successful.

sections.heading: Read what a chart records before interpreting a shape
sections.text:
A price chart summarises observations over a selected period. Depending on the display, a bar or candle may show an opening, high, low and closing price for an interval. The time interval, data source and adjustments matter. A one-day display and a multi-year display answer different questions. Learn the chart's definitions before assuming that a visible movement represents the same information across services or time frames.

An observation that price rose during an interval does not by itself explain why it rose or what will happen next. Several stories can fit the same shape after the event. Keep the historical description separate from a causal explanation and a forecast. A useful first chart note says what was observed, over which dates, with which source and what remains unknown. It does not turn a visually appealing pattern into certainty about the next price.

sections.heading: A last price can differ from the price available for your order
sections.text:
The chart often emphasises completed trades, while an order depends on current available interest and quantity. A last traded price does not guarantee an immediate transaction at that price. The spread, the age of a quote and the available size can be especially important when trading is infrequent. A line that looks smooth on a screen can conceal sparse observations or meaningful gaps between executable prices.

Imagine a security whose last trade was at KES 50, with current buying interest at KES 48 and selling interest at KES 52 in a simplified display. An immediate purchase and sale at those two levels would lose KES 4 per share before explicit costs. The chart's last price does not remove that gap. This invented example is a reminder to investigate execution rather than assuming that every point on a historical line was available to every order in any desired size.

sections.heading: Check adjustments and comparability
sections.text:
A change in a share's number of units, a distribution or another corporate event can affect how a historical series is presented. Different services may display adjusted or unadjusted prices under different conventions. Read the data provider's explanation before interpreting a large visible jump or comparing two charts. A change in the unit being measured is not automatically a gain or loss of the same size for an owner.

For a simple two-for-one split, the number of shares doubles while proportional ownership is unchanged. A chart that does not make the comparison basis clear can encourage a mistaken story about wealth disappearing overnight. This does not mean that every sudden move is a data adjustment. It means that the event and the presentation should be checked. Keep the original source, dates and adjustment convention beside any figure used in a practice hypothesis or a comparison of returns.

sections.heading: Test a hypothesis without borrowing future information
sections.text:
If you examine a historical pattern, state the rule before looking at the later result. Using information that was not available at the decision time creates look-ahead bias. Selecting only companies that survived or only the most attractive examples creates other distortions. A rule that looks successful after many alternative patterns have been tried can also reflect selection rather than a reliable relationship.

Write down the observation window, the decision rule, the time of the hypothetical entry and exit, and a plausible treatment of costs and execution. Include unsuccessful cases and explain missing data. A chart-based exercise in this classroom is not a validated trading system. It can help you learn how to formulate and challenge a claim. Treat a small or carefully selected historical sample as an invitation to further testing, not as evidence that an uncertain future price has become predictable.

sections.heading: Bring the chart back to the decision's purpose
sections.text:
Ask why a particular chart observation matters to the decision you are considering. An investment case about a company's long-term cash generation still needs business and valuation evidence. A shorter-horizon hypothesis still needs executable instructions, costs and risk analysis. A visually simple indicator does not replace those requirements. More lines on a chart can add complexity without adding independent information.

Finish an exercise with three separate sentences: what the chart records, what interpretation you are considering, and what would challenge that interpretation. Add a fourth sentence naming an execution issue the chart does not resolve. This format makes it easier to spot where a description has been stretched into an unsupported prediction. A disciplined conclusion can be that the picture is interesting but insufficient. Learning to describe the limits of an observation is part of becoming more capable, even when the resulting decision is to wait.

example.title: Four prices, an incomplete story
example.text:
A fictional daily bar opens at KES 30, reaches KES 33, falls to KES 29 and closes at KES 31. Those four prices do not tell you the exact sequence of every trade, whether you could fill a large order, or what tomorrow’s price will be.

Take a fictional chart ending at a last trade of KES 50. A separate current quote shows a KES 48 bid and KES 52 offer. Describe those observations without claiming that every order can transact at KES 50. An immediate purchase at the offer followed by a sale at the bid would lose KES 4 per share before explicit charges, under the simplified conditions. Now suppose the historical chart contains a share split. Ask whether the series is adjusted before interpreting an apparent price jump as a loss of wealth. Finally, write a pattern rule using only information available at a stated historical decision time. If the rule depends on seeing the later result first, it is not a fair test of what could have been known. Keep these data, execution and testing questions separate from any story about a guaranteed next move.

sections.heading: Write the decision before the outcome
sections.text: Record the hypothesis, supporting evidence, timeframe, proposed exposure and relevant costs before placing an order. Define what would contradict the idea and how you would respond. Avoid writing rules afterwards to justify the result.

sections.heading: Plan for difficult execution
sections.text: An intended exit is a decision rule, not a guaranteed transaction. Consider a price gap, an unfilled order or loss of access. Understand the provider’s cancellation procedures and order support; do not assume an order type exists because a foreign video demonstrates it.

sections.heading: Include a pause rule
sections.text: Specify circumstances in which you will not act: missing information, costs that overwhelm the idea, inability to monitor, or a strong urge to recover a loss immediately. There is no requirement to trade every day.

sections.heading: Write a plan that another learner could reconstruct
sections.text:
A useful plan identifies the decision, the evidence, the intended horizon, the security, the hypothetical quantity and the conditions under which no action will be taken. It should explain why the evidence is relevant rather than merely listing an indicator or a company name. Include the source and date of important facts. A second learner should be able to distinguish your observations from your expectations without asking you to fill in the missing story later.

Keep the plan short enough to use, but specific enough to challenge. “Buy because the market is strong” does not establish what strong means, which evidence matters or when the idea is wrong. A better exercise describes the conditions you are investigating and the information still needed. The plan is a record of a conditional decision, not a contract with the market. Writing it before an order helps prevent a later outcome from quietly becoming the reason you claim to have acted.

sections.heading: Include an execution checklist, not just an entry idea
sections.text:
Before a real instruction, the order preview and supported service should match the intended security, direction, quantity, price conditions and duration. Available cash, holdings and charges need to be understood. A plan should also identify how status will be checked and how an uncertain or interrupted instruction will be investigated. Do not assume that a request to cancel has succeeded until the relevant confirmation is available.

For practice, describe what you would do if an order filled only partly or did not fill. Decide which facts would need checking before sending another instruction. The classroom fills eligible orders instantly at fixed example prices, so it cannot test every branch of that checklist. You can still rehearse the questions. A well-written plan acknowledges the difference between the simple exercise and the real service rather than treating a smooth simulator experience as proof that the execution analysis is complete.

sections.heading: Define downside assumptions and their limits
sections.text:
State the amount exposed and the assumptions used to discuss a possible loss. If an exit condition is part of the hypothesis, explain whether it refers to evidence, a price observation or an available order service. The same word can conceal different actions. A price trigger, a manually reviewed thesis and an executable instruction do not necessarily behave alike. Check the intermediary's actual arrangements before assuming that a plan can be implemented as written.

Describe an adverse case that is worse than the preferred model. Prices can gap, liquidity can be limited and costs can matter more than expected. A stop or limit feature, where supported, does not remove every uncertainty. An invented loss budget is an educational input, not an assessment of what you personally should risk. A plan should make its limitations visible so that a precise-looking number does not create false confidence about an outcome that remains uncertain.

sections.heading: Prepare pause rules for information and behaviour
sections.text:
Some of the most useful plan conditions concern when to stop, not when to enter. Examples for a learning exercise include unclear account ownership, an unverified charge, contradictory data, a missing report or an inability to explain the business. Emotional pressure can also be recorded: rushing to recover a loss or acting because others appear successful can interfere with the process. A pause rule is a prompt to investigate, rather than a promise to avoid every future mistake.

Write the practical action that follows the pause. You might obtain the current tariff, verify an entity through the official register, compare the issuer's announcement with a summary, or step away and review the note later. A vague instruction to “be disciplined” is difficult to apply. A concrete information gap and a defined next research step are easier to review. Waiting can therefore be an active part of the plan, especially when the alternative is to conceal uncertainty behind a confident trade.

sections.heading: Review changes explicitly rather than moving the goalposts
sections.text:
New information can justify a changed decision. Record the new evidence, the date and the implication before changing the plan. Distinguish that process from altering the explanation simply because a price moved against you. If the intended horizon changes, explain why the new horizon has supporting evidence rather than treating it as an automatic way to avoid recognising a failed short-term idea.

After a practice trade, compare the record with the plan: security, quantity, assumed price, costs, reasons and review conditions. Identify one part that was followed and one part that needs improvement. Keep outcome and process separate. A favourable result can still reveal a weak instruction, while an adverse result can occur despite a carefully described decision. The point of a trading plan in this classroom is to create an honest basis for learning and review. It is not a formula that guarantees a profit or a certificate that the next real-money decision is appropriate.

example.title: A plan with a no-trade branch
example.text:
Suppose a hypothetical order only makes sense below KES 25. Before sending it, the available offer changes to KES 27. A written ceiling lets you reassess or pass; it does not require chasing the new price because you have already spent time on the idea.

Draft an invented plan for researching a small manufacturer. State which report you will read, the information needed about financing, an assumed cost basis and the circumstances that would make you wait. Do not choose a real order size for yourself from this exercise. Add an execution branch: if a hypothetical order partly fills, what status and records must be checked before another instruction is sent? A cancellation request alone does not establish that the remaining quantity has been cancelled. Then add a review branch: if new information contradicts the original reason, explain how the decision will be reassessed and dated. The plan should make it possible to distinguish new evidence from an attempt to avoid acknowledging an earlier mistake. A well-supported decision to do nothing is an acceptable final outcome of the exercise.

lessons.title: Keep a journal & measure results honestly
lessons.summary: Separate process, outcomes, costs and the limits of small samples.
outcomes: Calculate a basic net result
Understand why win rate alone is incomplete
Review errors without rewriting history

sections.heading: Record what was known at the time
sections.text: Keep the date, hypothesis, intended and actual prices, quantities, fees and reasons for acting. Include losing decisions and skipped opportunities. Preserve the original entry instead of editing it to match later events.

sections.heading: Look beyond a percentage of wins
sections.text: A high win rate can coexist with a net loss if occasional losses are large. Include costs and compare average gains with average losses. A short sample is not reliable proof that a process will work in future conditions.

sections.heading: Review the process as well as the money
sections.text: Ask whether you followed the written rules, whether assumptions were realistic and whether results depend on a few unusual outcomes. Paper results cannot reproduce all execution constraints or the experience of risking money.

sections.heading: Preserve the original reasoning and label later additions
sections.text:
A useful journal separates what was known at the decision time from what became apparent later. Record the reason, the source of evidence, the intended horizon and the principal uncertainty. If the note is written after the trade, say so. Human memory can make an outcome seem more predictable than it was. Keeping a dated original explanation helps you examine that tendency without pretending that a journal can eliminate it.

When new information arrives, add a review instead of silently rewriting the original thesis. A sentence such as “I now think the cost assumption was incomplete” tells a different story from claiming that you expected the outcome all along. The classroom journal lets you edit a reflection, so use the fields honestly and retain your own record of important earlier reasoning when needed. Avoid putting passwords, identity documents or sensitive account access information into the note. The goal is a useful learning record, not an unsecured store of personal credentials.

sections.heading: Separate observations, interpretations and future actions
sections.text:
An observation describes evidence: an account recorded a quantity, an issuer published a report or a hypothetical price differed from an assumption. An interpretation explains what you think that evidence means. A future action describes what you plan to investigate or change. Mixing all three into one confident sentence can make a review difficult to challenge. Label them so another learner can follow the reasoning.

For an invented practice buy, you might observe that KES 250 of virtual cash was used, interpret that as confirmation of the quantity calculation, and plan to examine fees with the calculator. That does not establish that the underlying share is attractive or that a real order would fill identically. A strong journal entry can therefore record a limited successful exercise without making a larger unsupported claim. Write what the simulator cannot show alongside what it did show.

sections.heading: Review the size of wins and losses, not only the win rate
sections.text:
Consider an invented set of 20 trades with 16 gains of KES 20 and four losses of KES 100. The gains total KES 320 and the losses KES 400, leaving a KES 80 loss before costs. If an assumed KES 2 cost applies to each trade, another KES 40 is removed, giving a KES 120 loss. An 80% win rate is compatible with this negative result because the losing outcomes are much larger.

The corresponding arithmetic average per trade is 0.8 times 20 minus 0.2 times 100, or minus KES 4 before the assumed cost. This is a description of the invented sample, not a reliable estimate of a future strategy's performance. Sample size, selection, execution and changing conditions still matter. Keep the full record and the cost basis rather than reporting only the most flattering statistic. Ask whether the data support the claim being made and what evidence would be needed to investigate it further.

sections.heading: Look for process patterns without manufacturing a trading edge
sections.text:
Review several notes for recurring information gaps or mistakes. Perhaps charges were repeatedly omitted, the intended horizon was unclear, or a source was accepted without checking its date. Those are useful process findings even if the sample cannot establish profitability. A few profitable outcomes do not demonstrate that a pattern is repeatable, and a spreadsheet of precise percentages does not solve the problem of an unrepresentative record.

Choose one improvement that can be observed in the next exercise, such as recording both sides of the tariff or writing a reason to wait. Avoid changing many rules at once and then claiming that the next outcome proves which change worked. Separate the question “Did I follow the process?” from “Was the result favourable?” This makes review more informative and less dependent on finding a story that flatters the latest trade. A journal supports reflection; it is not evidence that every conclusion drawn from it is correct.

sections.heading: Keep a usable record across resets and reviews
sections.text:
The classroom journal retains a snapshot of the practice trade linked to an entry. That allows a reflection to remain understandable if the practice portfolio is reset or an older trade leaves the recent history display. The snapshot is educational data, not an official contract note or a securities statement. For real activity, obtain and reconcile the records provided through the relevant account arrangements as well as keeping your own reasoning notes.

Use the reviewed flag after adding a meaningful lesson learned, rather than as a way to make a counter look impressive. Exported journal data can help you retain a private copy of the learning record, but the export is not an account-restoration system. Check what the file contains and protect it if you have included personal details. A useful review ends with a question or a specific improvement you can revisit. The quality of that reflection matters more than how many entries are marked complete.

example.title: Seven wins can still lose overall
example.text:
In ten invented trades, seven earn KES 100 each and three lose KES 300 each. The result is 700 − 900 = −KES 200 before any additional costs. A 70% win rate did not produce a profit. This is an arithmetic illustration, not a strategy test.

Use the invented twenty-trade record to challenge an attractive statistic. Sixteen wins of KES 20 produce KES 320, four losses of KES 100 remove KES 400, and a KES 2 assumed cost on each trade removes another KES 40. The final result is minus KES 120 even though sixteen of twenty trades won. The journal should show the full record and assumptions rather than only the win rate. Now write an honest review of one trade entered without checking costs. Preserve what was known at the time, describe the omission and specify the next action, such as obtaining a complete tariff before the next exercise. Do not rewrite the original reason to claim you anticipated the later outcome. This is a process-improvement exercise; neither a small positive record nor a well-organised journal proves a repeatable profitable strategy.

lessons.title: Capstone: defend a decision, not a prediction
lessons.summary: Bring research, execution and risk into a decision you can explain.
outcomes: Build a written decision case
Identify what the simulator cannot test
Recognise the limits of a course-completion badge

sections.heading: Assemble the evidence
sections.text: Select a fictional company or a historical case. Record the reporting period, the business model, relevant figures and your sources. Explain the intended horizon, valuation questions, costs and risks. Include a reasonable case against your own view.

sections.heading: Test your understanding
sections.text: Describe how you would place, change and reconcile an order. Explain what happens if it does not fill, the price gaps, a dividend changes or new information contradicts the original reason. Identify which features are absent from our simplified simulator.

sections.heading: Keep learning after completion
sections.text: Finishing these classes records learning progress, not professional competence, a financial qualification or an expectation of profit. Advanced development requires sustained practice, feedback and current knowledge of the market in which you operate.

sections.heading: Build a case from evidence someone else can inspect
sections.text:
Choose a fictional business or a clearly identified historical case for the capstone. Describe what it sells, who pays it, the resources it needs and the risks that matter to the explanation. Identify the reporting period and units of every figure you use. If you use a real company's published documents for practice research, keep the source links and do not present your classroom interpretation as the company's own conclusion or as a recommendation to other investors.

Create an evidence table with a claim, a source, its date, your interpretation and an unresolved question. A strong table includes evidence that challenges the preferred idea. Do not fill a gap with a guess merely because a final case needs to look complete. “This important item remains unexplained” is an honest finding. The purpose of the capstone is to connect research, valuation, execution and review in a case that can be questioned, not to produce the most confident forecast.

sections.heading: Explain the price question through more than one scenario
sections.text:
State the valuation approach and the assumptions it depends on. A ratio comparison, a present-value exercise and a business narrative answer related but different questions. Keep the relevant share count, earnings definition, financing structure and time period clear. Do not blend quantities from different methods simply to reach a preferred result. The evidence should determine what can reasonably be said, including where a simple method is not sufficient.

Write a less favourable scenario as carefully as the preferred one. What happens if revenue disappoints, costs rise, a major customer leaves or financing conditions become less helpful? These are invented analytical scenarios unless supported by specific evidence; they are not forecasts. Explain how the conclusion depends on the assumptions and what information would make you revise it. A range of conditional outcomes can be more useful than a single number that hides substantial uncertainty behind a neat presentation.

sections.heading: Connect an idea to an executable, cost-aware process
sections.text:
Describe the hypothetical instruction and the information needed to place it: security, direction, quantity, supported order type and relevant price or duration conditions. Include the cost assumptions and how status and final records would be checked. Explain what would happen if the order waited, filled partly or did not fill. Do not assume that the classroom's immediate fixed-price execution establishes the conditions in a real account.

Then reconcile a small practice example. Show the initial virtual cash, gross amount, resulting holdings and remaining cash. Add a separate realistic-cost scenario using clearly invented assumptions or a dated actual tariff if you have obtained one. Keep those two models separate so a zero-fee classroom result is not presented as a net real-world outcome. A defensible case needs a coherent path from the research idea to the instructions, resources and records required to carry it out.

sections.heading: Show the downside and the reasons you would wait
sections.text:
Identify the main ways the case could fail and the information you have not established. Distinguish an adverse business result, a lower market price, limited trading liquidity and an operational account problem. If an exit assumption is used, explain its limits. A trigger price does not guarantee an execution price, and a price boundary can leave an order unfilled. The actual services and rules must be confirmed with the intermediary.

Write explicit no-action conditions for the exercise. Examples include unclear charges, an unverified provider identity, a misunderstood debt item or evidence too weak to support the intended horizon. These are prompts for further investigation, not a personalised suitability assessment. The capstone should make it possible to see why waiting might be the best documented outcome of the research. Acting is not automatically more advanced than pausing, and a lucky price move does not retrospectively supply evidence that was missing at the time.

sections.heading: Invite a challenge and plan the next learning cycle
sections.text:
Ask another learner to identify the weakest assumption, reproduce one calculation and locate one of your cited sources. Invite a reasonable case against your view. Record the questions raised and distinguish corrections to factual errors from disagreements about uncertain assumptions. The exercise becomes more valuable when it can withstand examination or show clearly where it cannot, rather than when it avoids challenge.

Finish with a review plan: which information will be updated, what would change the case, and which topic you need to study next. Completing the classroom records educational activity. It does not establish a professional qualification, authorise advice to others or demonstrate that a strategy will be profitable. Continue with the credited books, official Kenyan resources and more demanding exercises at an appropriate pace. A capable learner can explain a decision, reconcile its records, acknowledge its limitations and identify the next question without promising an outcome the evidence cannot guarantee.

example.title: A defensible decision can be “not yet”
example.text:
If you cannot verify a provider’s charges or explain the business’s debt, a useful conclusion is to investigate further. A well-documented decision to wait can demonstrate more understanding than an unsupported prediction that happens to be right.

Prepare a fictional case for River Milling. Its product is understandable, but the available summary leaves a major debt item unexplained. A learner predicts that the share price will rise because recent sales look strong. Ask for the actual reporting period, cash-flow evidence, financing terms, relevant valuation assumptions and a cost-aware execution plan. Until the debt question is resolved, “investigate further” can be the most defensible conclusion. Invite another learner to reproduce one calculation and locate one source, then record the strongest argument against the preferred view. Include what the simulator cannot test, such as changing liquidity, actual charges or settlement. The capstone is successful when the reasoning and limits can be examined. It is not made more advanced by forcing a buy decision, claiming professional status or attaching a precise target price unsupported by the evidence.

faq.question: How does the help chat work?
faq.answer: Study help offers a built-in guide and an AI tutor when activated. The AI tutor requires a verified learning account and an open lesson section. It explains original teaching simply, uses different examples and asks guiding questions. It does not select or check quiz answers. The service label tells you which mode is replying. AI replies can be mistaken; verify the linked readings. AI questions and short lesson conversations are sent to OpenAI only in AI mode. Clear conversation removes the chat’s short server memory; chat history is not synced between devices.

faq.question: How do the module tests and final exam work?
faq.answer: Read and practise at your own pace. Each formal module test has 10 true/false questions and requires 100% to unlock the next module. The final has 15 single-answer questions and 10 questions with four independently marked true/false statements. It carries 55 marks; at least 47 marks meets the 85% pass mark. Formal questions allow two minutes each, including all four statements in a Section B question. Next records and locks the answer, and feedback appears only after the attempt ends.
faq.attribution: Soma na Mbiti classroom assessment policy.

faq.question: When can I retake an assessment?
faq.answer: Module tests allow five attempts. The final allows a first sitting and one retake after a failure. If all allowed attempts fail, study for seven days from the last failed attempt before a fresh set opens. Lessons remain available during the study break. Passed tests remain on record.
faq.attribution: Soma na Mbiti classroom assessment policy.

faq.question: Will I receive a student number and certificate?
faq.answer: A verified account receives a permanent student number. Complete your basic learner profile in My account and check your certificate name before starting the final. After passing all four module tests and the final, download your completion certificate from My account. The current signatory is Edwin Mbiti, Director & CEO, Soma na Mbiti. The certificate records classroom completion, rather than a professional licence.
